entities.name: John of Segovia
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
John of Segovia (c. 1395 – June 2, 1458) was a pivotal Castilian prelate, theologian, and canonist whose career spanned the tumultuous landscape of the 15th-century Western Schism and the burgeoning intellectual currents of early humanism. As a leading figure at the Council of Basle, he championed conciliarism—the doctrine asserting the authority of general councils over the Pope—a stance that defined his public life and eventually led to his exile. His intellectual curiosity, particularly his engagement with Islamic thought through the translation of the Quran, marks him as a significant bridge-builder between Christian and Islamic scholarship during a period of intense religious and political friction.

Educated at Salamanca, John of Segovia rose to prominence as a professor of theology and canon law before his appointment as a representative of the University of Salamanca at the Council of Basle in 1432. There, he became a fervent advocate for conciliar supremacy, playing a crucial role in drafting decrees against Pope Eugenius IV and participating in the election of the antipope Felix V. His diplomatic skills were evident in his missions to various European courts, including those of Emperor Frederick III and King Charles VII of France, seeking support for the council's agenda. Following the council's collapse and the eventual abdication of Felix V, John found himself increasingly isolated, settling in Savoy under the patronage of Duke Louis. It was there, in his final years, that he embarked on his most unique project: commissioning the first accurate Spanish translation of the Quran from the Muslim scholar Isa of Segovia, which he subsequently translated into Latin.
